ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in RetentionSweeper.sweep, which concatenates bucket and keepDays into the SELECT
ruled_out.killed_by: Both values are server-authored configuration, not attacker-controlled: bucket and keepDays are read from config.json:19-21 through the constructor at RetentionSweeper.java:32-33, and no request path writes them. Rule 13 requires an ingress point for attacker control and there is none.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in MetadataRepository.listByOwner, which String.formats the sort column into the statement
ruled_out.killed_by: The mitigation works. sort arrives as a SortColumn enum whose parse() (lines 35-42) matches the raw string against the three declared members and falls back to CREATED_AT on no match, so only 'created_at', 'title' or 'byte_size' can ever reach the format string. limit is an int.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in BlobStore.readPreset from the caller-supplied preset name
ruled_out.killed_by: readPreset maps the name through the fixed PRESETS map (lines 20-23) and returns a failed future for anything not in it, so the value reaching resolve() is one of three literal filenames. Contrast with resolve(), which is reported.

ruled_out.assertion: Unhandled NumberFormatException on the limit query parameter crashes the search handler
ruled_out.killed_by: Rule 07 excludes robustness and resource-exhaustion complaints unless the module exists to defend against DoS. A malformed limit yields a 500 on the attacker's own request and nothing more.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in reconcile.archive_report, which runs subprocess with shell=True
ruled_out.killed_by: The mitigation is real and correct: every element is passed through shlex.quote before the join (line 75), and dest_prefix is separately constrained to alphanumeric-plus-dash-underscore and 64 characters by validate_conf at lines 34-38, which gates the whole DAG.

ruled_out.assertion: Unsafe deserialization in transforms.read_cache, which calls pickle.load
ruled_out.killed_by: No attacker-controlled writer reaches the file today: _cache_path (line 24) strips everything outside [a-z0-9_] so the name cannot traverse, and the only writer is write_cache in the same module. The one route that could plant a file there is the extractall flaw, which is reported on its own and names this as a downstream consequence rather than a separate finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in the per-region rollup BashOperators
ruled_out.killed_by: The templated values are not attacker-controlled: params comes from settings.REGIONS and settings.WORK_ROOT (ledger_sync.py:76), both module constants, and ds is Airflow-generated. Unlike wait_for_close, no dag_run.conf value enters this command.

ruled_out.assertion: SSRF in reconcile.compare_totals, which fetches a URL built from the run payload
ruled_out.killed_by: Two working controls: the partition is validated against PARTITION_RE and the region allowlist by validate_conf (reconcile.py:31-42) before it is substituted, and fetch_reference enforces settings.ALLOWED_FETCH_HOSTS at hooks.py:51-53. The host is a fixed literal in the format string.

ruled_out.assertion: Open redirect or arbitrary launch through DeepLink.followNext
ruled_out.killed_by: followNext checks target.host against _trustedHosts before launchUrl (line 34) and returns false otherwise. The mitigation works; the unchecked parameter in that file is proof_url, which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded map tile API key in the Flutter client
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is a publishable client-side token, documented as scoped to the vendor's tile endpoints and embedded in the vendor's own web demo, and the identifier itself is prefixed pk. (publishable). Reporting a public-by-design key as a secret would be the hardcoded-mock case rule 02 excludes.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in ToolBox.sql_console, which concatenates the query into cur.execute
ruled_out.killed_by: Reachability was traced rather than assumed (rule 06) and the tool is absent from the available dict in registry() at tools.py:80-85, so dispatch returns 'unknown tool' and sql_console_enabled is never read; no other caller exists in the corpus. Reporting it would require hypothetical rewiring, which rule 01 excludes.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the retrieval layer's f-string query
ruled_out.killed_by: The interpolated schema name is configuration-sourced and the k parameter passes through int() twice, so no attacker-controlled value reaches the statement.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection through shell_exec in AdminController
ruled_out.killed_by: No HTTP ingress reaches the shell: $unit comes from getenv('LOG_UNIT') (config/settings.php:38) and $lines is int-cast and clamped. Rule 13 requires a cited attacker-controlled source and there is none.

ruled_out.assertion: PHP type-juggling authentication bypass on the loose != digest comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: Not strictly triggerable: the juggle needs BOTH sha256 hex strings to be numeric strings, and the attacker cannot influence the stored digest. The timing side is not exploitable either, since it cannot help invert sha256.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the sort, dir and limit parameters of the ticket list query
ruled_out.killed_by: The mitigations work: Sanitize::sortColumn allowlists strictly, direction collapses to ASC/DESC, and limit is int-cast and clamped. The injectable parameter in the same statement is status, which IS reported.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through column-name concatenation in Db::update
ruled_out.killed_by: Backtick-stripping prevents identifier breakout, so the injection class is blocked. The real defect on that path is mass assignment, which is filed as its own finding rather than stretched into a second SQL-injection claim.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded fleet sandbox token in the Salt pillar
ruled_out.killed_by: Documented in-tree as a published vendor quickstart value that reaches only sandbox.fleetvendor.example over https; the agent_token on the same file is generated at render time by salt['random.get_str'](40).

ruled_out.assertion: Private deploy key committed in the Salt pillar
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is an ssh-ed25519 PUBLIC key, consumed by ssh_auth.present (users/init.sls:33-35), which is its correct home. Reporting it as an exposed secret would misread the artefact.

ruled_out.assertion: Grain-spoofing privilege escalation through the pillar top file
ruled_out.killed_by: The grain-matched assignment is identical to the '*' assignment, so spoofing a grain changes nothing about which pillar data the minion receives.

ruled_out.assertion: Unsafe YAML deserialization in the gateway's config loader
ruled_out.killed_by: server.py uses yaml.safe_load, the correct API. Flagging it would be pedantic linting of a safe standard library call. Note the contrast with edge-fleet-salt's fleetctl.manifest, which uses yaml.Loader on remote input and IS reported.

findings.title: Cross-tenant IDOR: GET /tickets/{id} and the attachment routes serve any ticket id with no tenant or ownership predicate
findings.evidence:
INGRESS: src/Controllers/TicketController.php:47  `$id = (int) $args['id'];`  (route GET /tickets/{id}, public/index.php:50)
SINK:    src/Controllers/TicketController.php:52  `               FROM tickets WHERE id = ?',`  - the predicate is the id alone.
The middleware does supply the tenant: src/Middleware/AuthMiddleware.php:64 `->withAttribute('tenant_id', (int) $session['tenant_id'])`, and the sibling method uses it - src/Controllers/TicketController.php:106 `'SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?',`. show() never reads it, and then dumps the whole comment thread at :62-63 keyed on the same unchecked id.
The attachment routes have the same gap: src/Controllers/AttachmentController.php:52 `$base = $this->settings['storage']['attachments'] . '/' . (int) $args['id'];` (download) and :70 (remove), with no lookup of who owns that ticket.
findings.impact: Any authenticated low-privilege user walks ids 1..N and reads every other tenant's ticket subject, body, requester, assignee and full comment thread - a total breach of tenant isolation in a multi-tenant helpdesk. Through the attachment routes the same user downloads any tenant's uploaded files and, via DELETE /tickets/{id}/attachments/{name}, deletes them (unlink at AttachmentController.php:76).
findings.recommendation: Scope the read by the authenticated tenant: add `AND tenant_id = ?` to the query at TicketController.php:51-53 and pass `$request->getAttribute('tenant_id')`, mirroring what update() already does at :106; return 404 on mismatch. In AttachmentController, resolve the ticket and verify its tenant_id against the request attribute before building $dir/$base at :24, :52 and :70.

triage.reason: Both methods are bound to registered routes (public/index.php:50, :53, :54); nothing hypothetical.
Reproducible by requesting any id outside the caller's tenant; the response is the full ticket row.
No adjacent mitigation is being stretched - there is no ownership check anywhere on this path, as opposed to update() which has one.
I looked for a mitigation and found the codebase's own working pattern in update() at :104-108; its absence in show() is the finding, not a reinterpretation of a control that works.
TicketController.php:47/49/52/101/104/106, AuthMiddleware.php:62-66 and AttachmentController.php:24/52/70 were printed and read.
Attacker-controlled data is the {id} path segment, read at TicketController.php:47 and AttachmentController.php:52/70.

scope.established_by: the ticket id is taken from the URL and used to select or serve data without any tenant_id or requester_id predicate, even though AuthMiddleware.php:63-64 publishes both
scope.narrowed_by: an authenticated session is required (the /tickets group is behind AuthMiddleware at public/index.php:55); the list endpoint (TicketController.php:34) and the update ownership check (:106) are correctly tenant-scoped, so this affects the single-ticket read and the attachment routes only

searched.for: whether the codebase authorizes ticket access anywhere, which would show the check exists and I misread show()
searched.found: update() does authorize: `SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?` at :106 with a 404 at :109-111; show() has no equivalent

searched.for: an implicit tenant scoping the middleware might apply to every query
searched.found: nothing of the kind - the middleware only sets user_id/tenant_id/role attributes at :62-65 and delegates; scoping is left entirely to each controller

searched.for: an ownership check on {id} before the directory is built
searched.found: none in any of the three methods; :24, :52 and :70 build the path directly from (int)$args['id']

findings.title: Unparameterised query-string concatenation in LegacySearchController::search (controller is not routed)
findings.evidence:
INGRESS: src/Controllers/LegacySearchController.php:24  `$q = (string) ($request->getQueryParams()['q'] ?? '');`
SINK:    src/Controllers/LegacySearchController.php:27  `                 WHERE subject LIKE '%" . $q . "%' OR body LIKE '%" . $q . "%'`
         src/Controllers/LegacySearchController.php:30  `$rows = $this->pdo->query($sql)->fetchAll();`
PDO::query() never prepares, so nothing binds. REACHABILITY, traced rather than assumed: public/index.php imports only AdminController, AttachmentController and TicketController (lines 7-9) and registers no route for this class - the three route blocks are at :47, :58 and :65. `grep -rn LegacySearchController` over the whole corpus returns only its own declaration at LegacySearchController.php:16. There is no HTTP path to this method as shipped.
findings.impact: Nothing today: no route reaches it. The moment anyone re-registers the old console route - which the class docblock at :12-15 says is the plan until the 2019 console is decommissioned - a single ?q= value yields UNION-based read of any table the support_app user can reach, with no tenant predicate at all (the query at :26-28 selects across all tenants by design, which is exactly why it was superseded).
findings.recommendation: Delete the controller. If the query shape must be preserved, replace :26-30 with a prepared statement binding `'%' . $q . '%'` twice via Db::all(), and add the tenant_id predicate that TicketController::index has at :34, so that re-wiring the route can never reintroduce the injection.

triage.reason: The defect is deterministic on any invocation of search(): the value flows to PDO::query with zero processing. It is NOT triggerable over HTTP today because no route registers the controller - that is why FP-08 is what carries this finding and why the severity is low rather than high.

I did not dismiss the file for being labelled legacy. I traced reachability explicitly (imports at public/index.php:7-9, all three route blocks, and a corpus-wide grep) and report the result as part of the finding.
This is exactly the carve-out: direct injection in the module's own logic, valid with no caller. The flaw is intrinsic to the method, independent of who calls it.
LegacySearchController.php:22-30 was printed and read line by line, as were public/index.php:7-9 and the route registrations.
Ingress cited at LegacySearchController.php:24 ($request->getQueryParams()['q']); it is request data by construction, even though no route currently supplies the request.

scope.established_by: the query-string value is concatenated into the SQL text and executed through PDO::query, which does not prepare
scope.narrowed_by: no route registers this controller - public/index.php:7-9 imports the other three only and a corpus-wide grep finds no other reference - so there is no HTTP path to it in the shipped application; severity reflects that

searched.for: a use-statement or route that would make this controller reachable
searched.found: nothing: the imports at :7-9 are AdminController, AttachmentController and TicketController, and the groups at :47, :58 plus the standalone route at :65 never mention LegacySearchController

searched.for: any other file constructing or dispatching to it (a second front controller, a test harness, a deploy script)
searched.found: one hit only, the class declaration at src/Controllers/LegacySearchController.php:16

searched.for: a connection-level setting that might blunt the injection
searched.found: ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false at :27, which prevents stacked statements but has no effect on PDO::query, and none on a UNION or boolean-based extraction

findings.title: Retrieved corpus chunks are concatenated into the privileged system turn with no sanitisation, while only the caller's report body is scrubbed
findings.class: Indirect prompt injection from retrieved documents into a tool-enabled turn
findings.evidence: Attacker ingress: promptbridge-mlflow/bridge/retrieval.py:45 `{"chunk_id": r[0], "title": r[1], "source_url": r[2], "text": r[3]}` -- rows from the chunks table, which the module docstring (retrieval.py:3-4) states are fed by "the resolution notes people type when they close a ticket, so the table grows on its own". That text is placed verbatim into the system turn: prompts.py:37 `"### {title} ({source_url})\n{text}".format(` inside render_context, called from prompts.py:50 `context=render_context(documents),` which fills SYSTEM_TEMPLATE (prompts.py:16-17, "Runbook excerpts retrieved for this incident:"). The asymmetry is explicit at server.py:85 `report["body"] = guardrails.strip_control_instructions(report.get("body", ""))` -- the user turn is scrubbed, and the documents passed on server.py:88 are not. The same system turn advertises the callable tools (prompts.py:9 `{tool_manifest}`) and the completion is parsed for tool calls at server.py:100.
findings.impact: Anyone who can get text into the runbook corpus -- which by design includes anyone who closes a ticket -- writes instructions that the model reads inside the system turn, above the incident report, in the section the template calls house rules. Those instructions can emit `CALL calculator` (eval sink, tools.py:48) or `CALL http_fetch` (unrestricted SSRF, tools.py:36), so a planted document converts into code execution and internal network reads, repeated for up to max_tool_steps turns (server.py:99). Tool output is appended to the prompt (server.py:105) and returned to the caller (server.py:112), giving the attacker an exfiltration channel.
findings.recommendation: Treat retrieved text as untrusted data: run it through guardrails.strip_control_instructions (or a stronger filter) before render_context, fence each chunk in a clearly delimited data block that the system prompt instructs the model never to obey, and -- the part that actually holds -- stop trusting the model's tool line for privileged tools: require the tool call to be authorised out-of-band rather than parsed out of free text at tools.py:95.

triage.reason: The flow is the product's own main path: score() -> index.search() -> build_system() -> predict() -> dispatch(). No invented caller.

This is not missing hygiene in the abstract. The codebase sanitises the sibling field on the adjacent line (server.py:85), so the omission for retrieved text is a concrete gap on a reachable privileged path.
Triggerable: a chunk whose body contains a matching ticket keyword is returned by retrieval.py:39 and lands in the system turn on every scoring request for that incident.
retrieval.py:45, prompts.py:37/50, server.py:85/87/100/105/112 were read and re-printed by line number; render_context, SYSTEM_TEMPLATE and RunbookIndex.search all exist.
Attacker data enters at retrieval.py:45 (chunk body read out of the rag.chunks table populated by ticket resolution notes).

scope.established_by: Every /v1/score request calls index.search (server.py:79) and passes the result to build_system (server.py:87-88); there is no path that renders context from a trusted source only.
scope.narrowed_by: lookup_runbook (tools.py:51-54) returns chunks into the tool-result string rather than the system turn, so the system-turn placement is specific to the search path.

searched.for: a sanitisation call applied to `documents` between search and build_system
searched.found: nothing -- strip_control_instructions on line 85 is applied only to report['body'], and documents go untouched from line 79 to line 88

searched.for: escaping, fencing, or a trust marker separating retrieved text from instructions
searched.found: nothing -- chunks are joined with blank lines and pasted into the same template that carries the house rules and the tool manifest

searched.for: whether the filter would even hold if it were applied to retrieved text
searched.found: a five-phrase denylist anchored with ^\s* under (?im); trivially evaded by a leading quote character, altered wording or unicode lookalikes, so wiring it in is necessary but not sufficient

findings.title: The fleetops sudoers drop grants unrestricted passwordless root on every minion to a group that includes a contractor account
findings.evidence: The rule is written at edge-fleet-salt/salt/users/init.sls:22-27: `fleetops-sudoers:` / `  file.managed:` / `    - name: /etc/sudoers.d/fleetops` / `    - contents: |` / `        %fleetops ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` / `    - mode: '0440'`. The declared need is narrower than the grant — :20-21 `# On-call needs to restart the proxy and drain a node without waiting for a` / `# password prompt in the middle of an incident.` — two operations, against a rule that permits every command as every user with no re-authentication. The membership comes from pillar at :1 `{% set users = salt['pillar.get']('users', {}) %}` and :8-11 `{% for member in users.get('fleetops_members', []) %}` ... `    - name: {{ member }}`, resolving to edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:34-37 `  fleetops_members:` / `    - agata.ruiz` / `    - marek.solis` / `    - contractor.nightshift`. The state is applied fleet-wide: edge-fleet-salt/salt/top.sls:1-3 `base:` / `  '*':` / `    - users`.
findings.impact: Three accounts, one of them a contractor, hold unconditional root on every node in the fleet with no password re-prompt. Compromise of any one of those accounts — a stolen SSH key, a hijacked contractor workstation — is immediately full root on all minions, with no second factor between the shell and the privilege, and the NOPASSWD makes the escalation silent and non-interactive (scriptable by malware that lands in the session). The blast radius is the whole fleet because top.sls targets '*'.
findings.recommendation: Replace the ALL grant at :26 with the two commands the comment actually describes, e.g. `%fleetops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart nginx, /usr/bin/telemetry-agent drain *`, using absolute paths and no shell wrappers. Separately, move contractor accounts to their own group with a shorter command list and an expiry, rather than sharing the permanent on-call group.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is imagined. The grant is a literal in the managed file, and the members are enumerated in the pillar the state actually reads.

Not hygiene-only: the tree states the required privilege (restart the proxy, drain a node, :20-21) and grants a strictly larger one (ALL), with a named over-privileged principal (contractor.nightshift, pillar/fleet.sls:37). The gap between required and granted is the finding, not a style preference.
Reproducible: after highstate, any fleetops member runs `sudo -n id` on any minion and gets uid=0 with no prompt.
Applicability was traced rather than assumed: salt/top.sls:2-3 applies the users state to '*', and pillar/top.sls:2-3 serves the users pillar to '*' as well, so the rule lands on every minion.

The mitigations present were checked and accepted for what they do: mode 0440 root:root (:27-29) correctly protects the file from tampering, and check_cmd visudo -c -f (:30) correctly prevents a malformed drop from locking out sudo. Neither narrows the grant, which is what this finding is about.
Verified by reading: users/init.sls:1, :8-11, :20-30; pillar/fleet.sls:31-37; salt/top.sls:1-3; pillar/top.sls:1-3.

The untrusted principal is the account set fed in from pillar at users/init.sls:1/:8 (pillar/fleet.sls:34-37), notably contractor.nightshift at :37; the privilege sink is the sudoers line at users/init.sls:26.

scope.established_by: The fleetops-sudoers state (:22-30) writing /etc/sudoers.d/fleetops, applied to '*' by salt/top.sls:2-3.
scope.narrowed_by: Excludes the user.present loop (:9-18) and the fleetops-group state (:3-6), which create ordinary accounts with /bin/bash and a correct require on the group — those are not the privilege defect.

searched.for: a Cmnd_Alias, a command list, a Defaults line (timestamp_timeout, requiretty), or a second sudoers drop that would narrow the ALL grant
searched.found: nothing — /etc/sudoers.d/fleetops is a single line and is the only sudoers file the tree manages

searched.for: a per-role or per-environment membership list that would keep the contractor off production nodes
searched.found: one flat fleetops_members list served to '*' (pillar/top.sls:2-3); contractor.nightshift is in it unconditionally, and the comment at pillar/fleet.sls:32-33 confirms the intent that everyone gets the same access on every node

searched.for: controls that might already contain the risk
searched.found: both work for their own purpose — visudo -c -f validates syntax, 0440 root:root protects the file — but neither restricts which commands the group may run; recorded so the grant is not credited with a mitigation it does not have

searched.for: a committed private key or other secret in the same state
searched.found: nothing reportable — the committed value is an ssh-ed25519 PUBLIC key used with ssh_auth.present, which is the correct place for one; deliberately excluded from this finding

findings.title: calculator tool evaluates a model-controlled expression with eval() behind an empty-__builtins__ sandbox
findings.class: Eval injection through an LLM tool call
findings.evidence: Sink: promptbridge-mlflow/bridge/tools.py:48 `"value": eval(expression, {"__builtins__": {}}, dict(_SAFE_MATH)),`. The argument arrives from the model completion: tools.py:95 `for name, raw_args in CALL_RE.findall(completion):`, tools.py:102 `args = json.loads(raw_args)`, tools.py:104 `results.append({"tool": name, "result": handler(**args)})`. `dispatch` is driven from promptbridge-mlflow/bridge/server.py:100 `calls = self.toolbox.dispatch(completion)` inside the loop bounded by max_tool_steps. The completion is produced from a prompt containing the caller's report body (server.py:92 via prompts.build_user) and retrieved corpus text (server.py:87), so the expression string is attacker-influenced. `calculator` is live: config.yaml:35 lists it under tools.enabled, and tools.py:87 admits exactly the enabled names.
findings.impact: `{"__builtins__": {}}` is not a sandbox. An expression that walks the object graph, e.g. via `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()`, recovers real builtins and loaded modules from inside the empty-globals frame, giving arbitrary Python execution in the gateway process. The attacker only needs the model to emit one `CALL calculator {"expression": ...}` line, which is exactly what a poisoned runbook chunk or a crafted report body induces; the result is then also fed back into the next turn (server.py:105) and returned to the caller in the "tools" field (server.py:112).
findings.recommendation: Do not use eval for arithmetic. Parse the expression with `ast.parse(expr, mode="eval")` and walk the tree, permitting only Constant/BinOp/UnaryOp with a fixed operator set and rejecting Attribute, Name, Call, Subscript and comprehensions outright, or drop the calculator tool from tools.enabled.

triage.reason: The caller is real and in-tree: server.py:100 -> tools.py:104 -> calculator, with calculator enabled in the shipped config.yaml:35.

findings.title: fleetctl.manifest deserialises the fetched manifest with the unsafe yaml.Loader, turning the manifest server into root code execution on the minion
findings.evidence: Untrusted data enters over the network at edge-fleet-salt/salt/_modules/fleetctl.py:37-38 `    url = url or _pillar("fleet:manifest_url")` / `    resp = requests.get(url, timeout=20)` — the URL defaults to the pillar value at edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:6 `  manifest_url: https://fleet.internal.example/manifests/edge.yaml`, and `url` is itself a caller-supplied parameter (:31 `def manifest(url=None):`). The response body reaches the sink at :41 `    return yaml.load(resp.text, Loader=yaml.Loader)`. In PyYAML `yaml.Loader` is the unsafe loader (the alias of UnsafeLoader): a body containing `!!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"]` is executed during construction. Execution modules run as root on the minion (module docstring :3-4). No schema check, no safe_load, and no type check of the returned object exists between :38 and :41.
findings.impact: Anyone who can serve or tamper with the manifest response — a compromised or misconfigured fleet.internal.example, an operator passing a different `url`, or anyone able to intercept that fetch — obtains arbitrary code execution as root on every minion that runs fleetctl.manifest. findings.recommendation: Replace :41 with `yaml.safe_load(resp.text)` (or `yaml.load(resp.text, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader)`), then validate the resulting structure against the expected manifest shape before use. The docstring's claim that the manifest is 'richer than plain key/value data' (:34-35) does not require Python object construction — nested maps and lists are fully supported by SafeLoader.

Triggerable by serving one response body containing a python/object/apply tag; yaml.Loader constructs it. No preconditions beyond the function running.
Not pedantic linting of a correctly used safe library: PyYAML is used with its explicitly unsafe loader, and the safe API (safe_load / SafeLoader) exists and is not used.
There is no mitigation to accept. HTTPS on the default URL protects transport only; it does not constrain what the server returns, and `url` can be overridden by the caller anyway.

findings.title: nginx trusts X-Forwarded-For from every address, so the /admin/ IP allowlist is bypassable by any internet client sending one header
findings.class: Reliance on untrusted input in a security decision
findings.evidence: The real-IP block trusts every peer: edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/files/nginx.conf.jinja:5-7 `real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For;` / `real_ip_recursive on;` / `set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0;`. With the trusted-proxy set equal to the whole address space, nginx rewrites $remote_addr from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header, and real_ip_recursive walks the chain until it finds an untrusted address — of which there are none — so it settles on the leftmost, entirely attacker-written value. That rewritten $remote_addr is what the operator-console access rule tests at :42-44 `    location /admin/ {` / `        allow {{ admin_cidr }};` / `        deny all;`, where admin_cidr is 10.42.7.0/24 (edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:28, passed in at edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/init.sls:27). The server is internet-facing at :15-16 `    listen 443 ssl http2;` / `    server_name edge.example;`, and /admin/ proxies straight through at :46 `        proxy_pass http://app_backend;`. Untrusted data enters as the client's own X-Forwarded-For request header, accepted from any source by :7.
findings.impact: Any client that can reach https://edge.example/admin/ sends `X-Forwarded-For: 10.42.7.5` and passes the allow rule, reaching the operator console proxied to app_backend. The comment at :3-4 ('Requests arrive through the regional load balancers, which append the caller address to X-Forwarded-For') describes the intended topology, but set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0 removes the very distinction the design depends on — nginx cannot tell an LB-appended hop from a client-forged one. The location block carries no other authentication (no auth_basic, no auth_request, no client certificate), so this single header is the whole control.
findings.recommendation: Replace `set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0;` at :7 with the actual load-balancer prefixes (one set_real_ip_from per prefix), so nginx only honours X-Forwarded-For from the LBs and forged headers from arbitrary clients are ignored. Independently, stop treating a source address as authentication for /admin/: add a real authentication layer (mTLS or auth_request) so the console does not fall open when the proxy chain is misconfigured.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is postulated. The rendered config, as written, accepts the header from any peer and uses the result in the access decision.
Reproducible with a single request: `curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.42.7.5' https://edge.example/admin/`. The bypass needs no timing, no race and no prior access.
The `deny all` at :44 is a working directive, but it is not stretched — it is the fallback that only fires when the allow at :43 misses, and the allow matches on the spoofed value.
The template's reachability was traced, not assumed: webproxy/init.sls:19-23 renders it to /etc/nginx/conf.d/edge.conf, and salt/top.sls:5-7 applies webproxy to roles:edge-proxy.
code_paths names the two lines that constitute the flaw — the over-broad trust at :7 and the security decision at :43 — not the whole server block.

Untrusted data is the client's X-Forwarded-For request header, admitted from any source address by nginx.conf.jinja:7 and promoted into $remote_addr by :5-6.

findings.title: The telemetry agent .deb is fetched over plaintext http:// with no source_hash and installed with dpkg -i as root
findings.class: Download of code without integrity check
findings.evidence: The package source is a cleartext URL: edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:23 `  agent_package_url: http://packages.internal.example/edge/telemetry-agent_3.4.1_amd64.deb`. It is read at edge-fleet-salt/salt/telemetry/init.sls:1 `{% set telemetry = salt['pillar.get']('telemetry', {}) %}` and used as a remote (non-salt://) source at :8 `    - source: {{ telemetry['agent_package_url'] }}` with no `source_hash` anywhere in the state (:5-10). The downloaded bytes are then executed as root at :12-14 `telemetry-agent-install:` / `  cmd.run:` / `    - name: dpkg -i /var/cache/fleet/telemetry-agent.deb`, ordered after the download by `require: - file: telemetry-agent-package` (:16-17). Contrast with the neighbouring webproxy state, which uses a master-served source with no such exposure: edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/init.sls:22 `    - source: salt://webproxy/files/nginx.conf.jinja`. Reachability: edge-fleet-salt/salt/top.sls:8 and :12 apply telemetry to both role groups.
findings.impact: Anyone positioned on the path to packages.internal.example — an ARP/DNS spoofer on the edge network, a compromised caching proxy, or anyone who can answer for that hostname — substitutes a .deb of their choosing, and every edge and collector node installs it as root via dpkg maintainer scripts. There is no checksum, no signature, and no TLS to detect the swap. The `unless: dpkg -s telemetry-agent` guard at :15 only checks that a package by that name is installed; it validates nothing about the file's contents.
findings.recommendation: Serve the package over https and pin it: add `- source_hash: sha256=<digest>` (or a `source_hash` URL) to the file.managed at :5-10, and change pillar/fleet.sls:23 to an https:// URL. Better, install through pkg.installed against a signed apt repository so dpkg/apt verifies the vendor signature instead of an unauthenticated file drop.

triage.reason: No hypothetical caller. The highstate itself downloads and installs; the flaw is in the declared state.

This is not missing hygiene around a safe operation — the missing integrity check is what stands between a network position and root code execution, and the http:// scheme makes that position sufficient.

findings.title: The fleet agent bearer token is written to /etc/fleet/agent.token world-readable (mode 0644)
findings.class: Incorrect permission assignment for critical resource
findings.evidence: The secret is written by edge-fleet-salt/salt/webproxy/init.sls:10-17: `fleet-agent-token:` / `  file.managed:` / `    - name: /etc/fleet/agent.token` / `    - contents: {{ fleet['agent_token'] }}` / `    - makedirs: True` / `    - user: root` / `    - group: root` / `    - mode: '0644'`. Mode 0644 is rw-r--r--: every local account on the node can read it. The value is the control-plane bearer credential — edge-fleet-salt/pillar/fleet.sls:8-10 `  # Written to /etc/fleet/agent.token on every edge node so the agent, the` / `  # metrics shipper and the log tailer can all read it.` / `  agent_token: '{{ salt["random.get_str"](40) }}'` — and the same pillar key is used as a Bearer header at edge-fleet-salt/salt/_modules/fleetctl.py:80-85 `    token = _pillar("fleet:agent_token")` ... `        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + str(token)},`. The stated requirement (three service accounts must read it, webproxy/init.sls:8-9) calls for a group, not for world-readable: the file is root:root (:15-16), so the three service accounts are served only by the world bit.
findings.impact: Any unprivileged local user or compromised service on an edge node reads the node's control-plane bearer token and can authenticate to https://fleet.internal.example/api/v1/enroll (pillar/fleet.sls:5) as that node — enrolling, re-enrolling or acting with the node's identity. This converts any low-privilege foothold on an edge proxy into fleet-level credential access, and the token is served to nodes fleet-wide because pillar/top.sls:2-3 assigns the fleet pillar to '*'. [calibrate] Severity lowered to medium: Reading the token requires an existing local foothold on the node, and the blast radius is the fleet agent credential rather than the control plane; the sub-agent scored it high on the secret's sensitivity alone.
findings.recommendation: Set `- mode: '0640'` and `- group: fleet` (or whichever group the agent, metrics shipper and log tailer share), adding the group with a group.present state and a require so ordering is guaranteed; keep the owner root. If the three consumers cannot share one group, give each its own 0600 copy rather than widening the mode.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is invoked. The state declares the mode; the file lands 0644 on every convergence.

Not hygiene-only: a bearer credential readable by every local account is a concrete access-control break with a named principal set (any local user) and a named capability (authenticate to the control plane).
Reproducible by running the highstate and stat-ing /etc/fleet/agent.token; the declared mode is a literal '0644' with no conditional.

findings.title: stage_csv chmods the staged ledger export to 0666 before the COPY step reads it
findings.class: Incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource
findings.evidence: transforms.py:90-91: the comment explains the intent -- 'The COPY runs as the postgres service account, not as the Airflow worker' -- and the code grants world read AND write: `os.chmod(path, 0o666)`. The file holds the normalised posting rows about to be loaded into ledger.postings (written lines 85-88) and lives in WORK_ROOT, /opt/airflow/work/ledger by default (settings.py:23). LedgerExportOperator then moves the same file to the finance share (operators.py:97-98).
